This document outlines the testing procedure P1, which must be performed 
 on a weekly basis 
 as indicated by W1 in the above title block

Copper salts are used in water supply systems to 
 control biological growths in reservoirs and distribution pipes and to 
 catalyze the oxidation of manganese. Corrosion of copper containing alloys in pipe fittings may introduce 
 measurable amount of copper into the water in a pipe system.

This document outlines the experiment used in copper concentration 
 determination. The experiment is known as copper neocoproine method.

The first draft initiated by chem. Mohamed A. Farrag, tested 
 by chem. Esam Abdel Aziz Mohamed, reviewed by director chem. Mohamed Kamal, 
 revised by EDEPCo. quality control chemist Wael A. Tantawy, and approved by 
 eng. Ahmed El-Refaey; Head Sector of Abu Sultan Power Station.

Cuprous ion in neutral or slightly acidic solutions reacts 
with neocoproine (2,9 dimethyl 1,10 phenanthroline) to form a yellow colored 
complex. The complex can be extracted by a number of organic solvents including 
a chloroform-methanol mixture. The reaction is virtually specific for copper; 
the colour follows Beer's law up to a concentration of 
0.2 mg Cu/25 ml solvent. The full colour development 
is obtained when the pH of the aqueous solution is between 3 and 9. The color is 
stable in CHCl3-CH3OH for several days.

Copper ion tends to be adsorbed on the surface of 
sample containers. Therefore, analyze samples as soon as possible after 
collection. If storage is necessary, use 0.5 mL 1+ 1 HCl / 100 mL sample to 
prevent this adsorption.

The 
minimum detectable concentration to 0.01 absorbance is 3 g Cu when a 1 cm cell 
is used and 0.6 g Cu when a 5 cm cell is used.

items:
The sample must be taken as the applicable ASTM methods D 
 3370-76.

Acids such 
 as hydrochloric acid and others are dangerous, so you have to wear breathing 
 mask.

Keep these 
 acids closed. Don't get it in the eyes, on the skin, or on clothing. Don't 
 breathe them, use only in a hood.

Store 
 ammonium hydroxide solution in polyethylene bottle.
Spectrophotometer for use at 457 nm, providing a light path of 1 cm or longer.
Separatory funnels 125 ml with glass or TFE stopcock and stopper.
Volumetric flasks 100 ml.
Hot plate.

Pipette 
 50 ml water into a 125 ml separatory funnel for use as a reagent blank.

Prepare 
 standards by pipetting 1.00 to 10.00 ml (20 to 200 g Cu) standard copper solution 
 into a series of 125 ml separatory funnel, and dilute to 50 ml with water. Add 
 1 ml conc. H2SO4 and use the extraction procedure (see 
 II ).

Construct 
 a calibration curve by plotting absorbance vs. g of Cu.

Dilute 
 10.0 mL standard copper solution to 100 mL. Carry 1.00 to 10.00 mL volumes of 
 this diluted standard through the extraction procedure (see II ), but 
 use 5-cm cells to measure absorbance.

Transfer 
 100 ml sample to a 250 ml beaker, add 1ml conc. H2SO4 and 5 ml 
 conc. HNO3.Add a few boiling chips and cautiously evaporate to dense white SO3 fumes 
 on hot plate .If solution remains colored, cool, add another 5 ml conc. HNO3 
 and again repeat if necessary, until so becomes colorless.

Cool, add 80 ml H2O and bring to a boil, cool and 
 filter into 100 ml volumetric flask and complete to 100 ml with water.

Pipette 50 ml or other suitable portion contains 4 to 200 g into 
 a 125 ml separatory funnel, add 5 ml Hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution and 
 10 ml sodium citrate solution, and mix thoroughly.

Adjust pH to 4 by adding NH4OH until Congo red 
 paper is just definitely red.

Add 10 ml neocoproine reagent and 10 ml chloroform. Stopper 
 and shake vigorously for 30 sec. to extract the copper neocoproine complex 
 into the chloroform.

Let mixture separate into two layers and withdraw lower layer 
 into a 25 ml volumetric flask taking care not to transfer any of the aqueous 
 layer and dilute to 25 ml with methanol, stopper ,mix

Transfer an appropriate portion of extract to a suitable 
 absorption cell (1cm for 40 to 200 g Cu; 5 cm for lesser amounts).
Measure absorbance at 457 nm or with 450-460 nm.

Determine micrograms copper in final solution by reference to 
 the appropriate calibration curve.
